title: AQA GCSE Physics · The Electromagnetic Spectrum

items.stem: Which statement best describes an electromagnetic wave?

options.text: A transverse wave that transfers energy from source to absorber
A longitudinal wave that transfers energy to an absorber
A transverse wave that transfers matter to an absorber
A transverse wave that needs air to carry its energy

items.why: The specification defines electromagnetic waves as transverse waves that transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber.

items.stem: How do the speeds of radio waves, visible light and gamma rays compare in a vacuum?

options.text: Gamma rays are fastest because they carry the most energy
Radio waves are slowest because their wavelength is longest
All of them travel at the same velocity in a vacuum
Visible light is faster than the radio waves are

items.why: All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.

items.stem: Which list gives the electromagnetic groups in order from longest wavelength to shortest?

options.text: Radio, microwave, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, X-rays, gamma
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Radio, microwave, infrared, violet, red, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma

items.why: This is the order given in the specification, going from long to short wavelength.

items.stem: The electromagnetic spectrum is described as continuous. What does this mean?

options.text: It is made of seven separate waves with gaps between them
It jumps in seven fixed steps like rungs on a ladder
Every group in it can be detected by the human eye
There are no gaps between one group and the next

items.why: Wavelength changes smoothly across the spectrum, so the groups merge into one another with no gaps.

items.stem: Moving across the spectrum from radio waves towards gamma rays, what happens to wavelength and frequency?

options.text: Wavelength decreases and frequency increases
Wavelength and frequency both increase together
Wavelength rises while the frequency falls
Both wavelength and frequency decrease

items.why: Going from long to short wavelength is the same as going from low to high frequency.

items.stem: A transmitter sends radio waves to a distant aerial. What is transferred, and in which direction?

options.text: Particles of matter, from the transmitter to the aerial
Energy, from the source of the wave to the absorber
Energy, carried along by the air between them
Sound, from the transmitter to the radio aerial

items.why: The wave transfers energy from the source (the transmitter) to the absorber (the aerial).

items.stem: A hot radiator emits infrared radiation. Why can a person in the room not see it?

options.text: The radiator is not hot enough to glow visibly yet
The eye can see infrared, but only in a dark room
Infrared travels too fast for the eye to detect
Our eyes only detect visible light, not infrared

items.why: Eyes only detect visible light and so detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves.

items.stem: Which of these is the best example of energy being transferred by an electromagnetic wave?

options.text: A loudspeaker making the nearby air vibrate
Warm air rising above a heater in a room
Sunlight warming a dark road surface
A spoon warming inside a mug of hot tea

items.why: The Sun is the source and the road is the absorber; energy crosses empty space as an electromagnetic wave.

items.stem: Which statement about how substances behave towards electromagnetic waves is correct?

options.text: A substance that fails to transmit a wave must have absorbed the whole of it.
One substance can reflect one wavelength but absorb a different one.
A wave behaves in just the same way in every substance it meets.
A clear substance will transmit every wavelength reaching it.

items.why: This is what the specification means by behaviour varying with wavelength: a single substance treats different wavelengths differently.

items.stem: A water wave crosses from deep water into shallow water at an angle to the boundary and changes direction. What causes the change of direction?

options.text: The wave bounces off the edge of the shallow part and is pushed aside.
The shallow water blocks part of the wave, so the rest swings round.
The two depths pull on the wave with different sideways forces.
The wave has a different velocity in the shallower water.

items.why: Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances.

items.stem: In a wave front diagram, what does each drawn line represent?

options.text: A line joining points of the wave that are all in phase.
A line drawn parallel to the direction the wave is travelling.
A line whose spacing is the same in every medium it enters.
A line that is spaced more widely wherever the wave moves slower.

items.why: A wave front joins points in phase, such as all the crests, and it lies at right angles to the direction of travel.

items.stem: A wave front diagram shows plane wave fronts meeting a boundary at an angle. The wave travels more slowly in the second medium. Why do the fronts change direction?

options.text: The whole of each front slows down at the very same instant it crosses.
The fronts turn because the ray drawn through them is refracted there.
One end of each front enters the slower medium first and is held back, so it pivots.
The fronts spread further apart in the slower medium, and that turns them.

items.why: While one end is slowed and the other is still at the original speed the front swings round, which is the wave front explanation of refraction.

items.stem: A sheet of window glass lets almost all of the visible light reaching it pass through, but it absorbs most of the ultraviolet. What does this show?

options.text: Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
A material that looks clear to the eye must be transmitting every wave reaching it.
Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.
Any wave the glass does not transmit must be completely absorbed by it.

items.why: Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength, and one substance treating two wavelengths differently is exactly that.

items.stem: Radio waves from a distant transmitter pass easily through the brick walls of a house, but visible light from outside does not. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Radio waves carry far more energy than light, so they force a way through brick.
Brick is not transparent, so no electromagnetic wave at all can cross it.
The brick transmits radio waves but reflects and absorbs the light.
The light is not transmitted, so the wall absorbs every bit of it.

items.why: The same substance behaves differently towards different wavelengths, which is precisely the variation with wavelength the specification describes.

items.stem: Light travelling through air enters a glass block, where it travels more slowly. Its frequency does not change. What happens to its wavelength?

options.text: It stays the same, because the wavelength is fixed by the lamp producing it.
It gets shorter, because the velocity falls while the frequency stays the same.
It gets longer, because a slower wave needs more time for each cycle.
It stays the same, because light has one fixed speed in everything.

items.why: With the velocity smaller and the frequency unchanged, the wavelength must fall, so the wave fronts sit closer together in the glass.

items.stem: A student is drawing a ray diagram for light passing from air into a glass block. Where should the angle of incidence be measured?

options.text: Between the incoming ray and the flat surface of the glass block itself.
Between the incoming ray and the refracted ray inside the block.
Between the incoming ray and the normal drawn at the point it enters.
Between the refracted ray and the flat surface of the block.

items.why: The normal is the dashed line at right angles to the boundary at the point of entry, and both angles are measured from it.

items.stem: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block along the normal, so the angle of incidence is 0°. What should the ray diagram show?

options.text: The ray bends towards the normal as it enters, then bends back as it leaves.
The ray bends away from the normal as soon as it crosses into the glass.
The ray bends sideways as soon as it enters the glass block.
The ray carries straight on through the block without changing course.

items.why: Along the normal every part of the wave front crosses the boundary at the same instant, so the wave slows but is not deviated.

items.stem: In Required practical activity 10 a Leslie cube is filled with hot water. An infrared detector is placed the same distance from each vertical face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?

options.text: All four read the same, because the water behind each face is at one temperature.
The shiny silver face, because polished metal gives out infrared best.
The matt white face, because pale surfaces give out the most radiation.
The matt black face, because matt black is the best emitter of infrared.

items.why: A good absorber is also a good emitter, so the matt black face radiates most strongly at that temperature.

items.stem: Four identical cans are painted matt black, matt white, shiny silver and dull grey. Each is filled with cold water and placed the same distance from a radiant heater. Which can's water warms fastest?

options.text: The shiny silver can, because a polished metal surface takes radiation in best.
The matt black can, because it is the best absorber of infrared.
All four cans equally, because the heater is the same distance away.
The dull grey can, because a metal surface draws radiation in fastest.

items.why: Matt black is the best absorber, so it takes in radiation from the heater at the greatest rate and warms fastest.

items.stem: A ray of light travels through air and strikes the flat surface of a glass block at an angle to the normal. Light travels more slowly in glass than in air. Which statement correctly describes the refracted ray inside the glass?

options.text: It bends towards the normal, because it slows down in the glass.
It bends away from the normal as it enters the glass.
It carries straight on undeviated, changing only its speed.
It reflects off the surface without entering the glass at all.

items.why: Air into glass is a change to a slower medium, and a ray slowing at an angled boundary bends towards the normal.

items.stem: A student compares the infrared radiation emitted by the four faces of a Leslie cube. Which change would most improve the investigation?

options.text: Keep the detector the same distance from every face when reading it.
Move the detector closer to the darker faces so their readings are clearer.
Take the reading from each of the faces at a different water temperature.
Use a separate metal cube for each of the four surfaces tested.

items.why: Distance is a control variable: the reading falls as the detector is moved away, so it must be fixed if only the surface is to change.

items.stem: (HT only) How can radio waves be produced?

options.text: By oscillations in an electrical circuit
By heating a metal aerial till it glows
By changes in the nucleus of the atom
By changes in the electrons of an atom

items.why: The specification states that radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

items.stem: (HT only) A radio wave is absorbed by an aerial joined to a circuit. What may the wave create in that circuit?

options.text: A steady direct current, always one way
An alternating current in that circuit
A magnetic field but no current in it
A current whose frequency is doubled

items.why: The specification states that absorbed radio waves may create an alternating current, so they induce oscillations in the circuit.

items.stem: Where do gamma rays originate?

options.text: In changes to the electrons of an atom
In bonds being broken between two atoms
In the heating of very dense material
In changes in the nucleus of an atom

items.why: The specification states that gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

items.stem: Ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays can have hazardous effects on human body tissue. What do those effects depend on?

options.text: The size of the dose received, whatever type it is
Only the total size of the dose, not its type
The distance the radiation travelled to the body
The type of radiation and the size of the dose

items.why: The specification states that the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.

items.stem: What effects can ultraviolet waves have on human body tissue?

options.text: Skin ages early and the risk of skin cancer rises
Genes mutate, as ultraviolet is ionising radiation
Skin ages early but the risk of cancer is unchanged
Skin ages early because the tissue gets heated

items.why: The specification states that ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.

items.stem: Which statement about how electromagnetic waves are generated and absorbed is correct?

options.text: Only changes in the nuclei of atoms can generate these waves
Changes in atoms and in their nuclei generate and absorb them
Only changes in the electrons of an atom can generate them
Atoms generate these waves but can never absorb any of them

items.why: The specification states that changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range.

items.stem: A worker's radiation dose is recorded in sieverts (Sv). What does this dose measure?

options.text: The number of nuclei decaying near the worker
The amount of radioactive material in the body
The risk of harm that results from the exposure
The frequency of the radiation entering the body

items.why: The specification states that radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.

items.stem: Why can X-rays and gamma rays cause cancer in human body tissue?

options.text: They are absorbed by the skin and make it age early
They are ionising and can cause genes to mutate
They heat body cells until those cells are killed
They are ionising, so they burn the skin surface

items.why: The specification states that X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

items.stem: (HT only) A transmitter sends out radio waves at 200 MHz. A receiving aerial absorbs them and an alternating current is created in the circuit joined to it. What is the frequency of that current?

options.text: 100 MHz, half the frequency of the wave
400 MHz, twice the frequency of the wave
200 MHz, the same as that radio wave
0 Hz, because the current is direct

items.why: The specification states that the alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself.

items.stem: A patient receives a radiation dose of 75 mSv from a scan. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). What is this dose in sieverts?

options.text: 7.5 Sv
75 Sv

items.why: 75 divided by 1000 gives 0.075 Sv, using the relationship 1000 mSv = 1 Sv as given in the stem.

items.stem: The table shows the average dose a person in the UK receives each year: radon gas 1.3 mSv, medical X-rays 0.4 mSv, cosmic rays 0.3 mSv. Which conclusion is supported by these data?

options.text: Medical X-rays give the largest yearly dose of the three
The three sources together give a dose of over one sievert
Radon gives a larger yearly dose than the other two added
Cosmic rays carry the greatest risk as they come from space

items.why: 1.3 mSv is greater than 0.4 mSv + 0.3 mSv = 0.7 mSv, so this conclusion does follow from the data given.

items.stem: Three workers received yearly doses of 6 mSv, 18 mSv and 0.5 Sv. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). Which worker is at the greatest risk of harm?

options.text: The worker on 18 mSv, the largest number shown
The worker on 6 mSv, since small doses build up most
All three equally, since 6, 18 and 0.5 are small
The worker on 0.5 Sv, because that equals 500 mSv

items.why: Converting with 1000 mSv = 1 Sv gives 500 mSv, far greater than 18 mSv or 6 mSv, so this dose carries the greatest risk.

items.stem: Which use does the specification give for radio waves?

options.text: Broadcasting television and radio programmes
Sending signals to and from satellites in orbit
Carrying signals along fibre optic cables
Taking images of bones inside the body

items.why: The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio.

items.stem: Which type of electromagnetic wave carries the signals in a fibre optic cable?

options.text: Visible light, sent as very rapid pulses
Microwaves, as used for satellite phone links
Radio waves, as used for television aerials
Infrared, which warms the glass fibre

items.why: The specification pairs visible light with fibre optic communications; information travels as pulses of light along the glass fibre.

items.stem: How does a microwave oven cook food?

options.text: Microwaves heat the middle of the food first
Microwaves make the food slightly radioactive
An element's red glow is the infrared that cooks it
The food absorbs microwaves and heats up

items.why: Microwaves are absorbed by the food, and the energy transferred raises its temperature.

items.stem: A sunbed is used to give a tan. Which statement about the radiation it uses is correct?

options.text: It gives out infrared, and the heat browns skin
It gives out visible light, which the skin absorbs
It gives out ultraviolet, which can harm skin
Its ultraviolet is safe because the dose is small

items.why: The specification pairs ultraviolet with sun tanning; ultraviolet darkens the skin but is absorbed by skin cells and can damage them.

items.stem: Why does a broken bone show up clearly on an X-ray photograph?

options.text: X-rays pass through bone but are absorbed by flesh
X-rays are reflected from the surface of the bone
X-rays make the bone give out light of its own
X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone

items.why: Bone absorbs X-rays far more strongly than flesh does, so a shadow of the bone, and of the break in it, falls on the detector.

items.stem: Gamma rays are used in hospitals to treat cancer. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Gamma rays leave the treated tissue permanently radioactive
Gamma rays are far too dangerous ever to be used here
A beam of gamma rays is aimed at the tumour to kill cells
Gamma rays are used only to photograph broken bones

items.why: The specification pairs X-rays and gamma rays with medical treatments; a directed beam destroys the cells of the tumour.

items.stem: (HT only) Explain why microwaves rather than infrared are used to send signals to a communications satellite.

options.text: Microwaves travel much faster through space than infrared can
Microwaves pass through the atmosphere, infrared does not
Infrared cannot cross the vacuum of space, but microwaves do
Microwaves are the only waves a dish aerial can send

items.why: The atmosphere transmits microwaves, so the signal reaches the satellite and returns; infrared is strongly absorbed by gases and water vapour in the air.

items.stem: (HT only) An energy efficient lamp produces ultraviolet inside its tube, yet the room is lit by visible light. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: A coating absorbs ultraviolet and emits visible light
The lamp is designed to send ultraviolet into the room
The ultraviolet itself is the light you see the room by
Ultraviolet slows down in the tube, becoming visible light

items.why: The fluorescent coating on the inside of the tube absorbs the ultraviolet and re-emits the energy as visible light, so the room is lit without ultraviolet leaving the lamp.

items.stem: The specification lists a practical application for each group of electromagnetic waves. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Satellite communication uses radio waves
Sun tanning lamps mainly give out infrared
Fibre optic communications use visible light
A toaster cooks bread using microwaves

items.why: The specification pairs visible light with fibre optic communications: the signal travels along the glass fibre as rapid pulses of light.

items.stem: A signal is sent from a ground station up to a satellite in orbit and then back down to a second ground station. Which waves carry the signal?

options.text: Radio waves, which are used for broadcasting today
Microwaves, which pass through the atmosphere
Infrared, which is given out by all hot objects
Visible light, which goes in straight lines

items.why: The specification pairs microwaves with satellite communications; the atmosphere transmits them, so they reach the satellite and return.

items.stem: An electric grill glows red and cooks the food placed underneath it. Which radiation transfers energy to the food?

options.text: Microwaves, because all cookers use microwaves
Infrared, which is absorbed by the food surface
Ultraviolet, because the element glows white
Radio waves, because they carry heat energy

items.why: The specification pairs infrared with electrical heaters and cooking food; the hot element emits infrared, which the surface of the food absorbs.

items.stem: An infrared camera is used to find a person standing in a dark field at night. Why does the person show up on the image?

options.text: The camera shines visible light on the person
Infrared from the body can be seen by the eye too
The person reflects ultraviolet from the night sky above
Their body gives out infrared that the camera detects

items.why: The specification pairs infrared with infrared cameras; a warm body emits infrared, which the camera detects even in total darkness.

items.stem: Rays of light travelling parallel to the principal axis pass into a convex lens. What happens to these rays?

options.text: They are refracted and brought to a focus at the principal focus
They are reflected from the front face of the lens to a point
They are refracted and cross each other at the focal length
They pass straight through and bend only as they leave

items.why: This is what the specification states: in a convex lens, parallel rays of light are brought to a focus at the principal focus.

items.stem: What is meant by the focal length of a convex lens?

options.text: The distance from the lens to the object being viewed
The distance from the lens to the principal focus
The distance from the lens to the sharp image
The thickness of the lens where it is widest

items.why: This is the specification's definition: the distance from the lens to the principal focus is called the focal length.

items.stem: Which statement about the image formed by a concave lens is always true?

options.text: It is real if the object is far enough away
It is inverted, like the image from a lens
It is too faint for anyone to look at it
It is virtual, wherever the object is

items.why: The specification states that the image produced by a concave lens is always virtual, whatever the object distance.

items.stem: Which two quantities are needed to calculate the magnification produced by a lens?

options.text: The focal length of the lens and the object height
The distance to the image and to the object
The height of the image and the focal length
The height of the image and the object height

items.why: The specification gives magnification = (image height)/(object height), so the two heights are what is needed.

items.stem: A student measures both heights in centimetres and calculates a magnification of 2.5. How should this answer be written?

options.text: As 2.5 cm, keeping the unit of the heights measured
As 2.5 mm, since mm is a unit used for heights
As 2.5 m, because metres are the SI unit of length
As 2.5 on its own, because a ratio has no units at all

items.why: Magnification is a ratio and so has no units, so the answer is the bare number 2.5.

items.stem: In ray diagrams, which symbol is used to represent a convex lens?

options.text: A vertical line with two arrowheads pointing inwards
A vertical line with outward arrowheads at each end
A shape drawn curved outwards on each of its two faces
A vertical line with a single inward arrowhead

items.why: The convex lens is drawn as a straight vertical line whose arrowheads point outwards, matching the outward bulge of the lens.

items.stem: Which symbol is used in a ray diagram to represent a concave lens?

options.text: A line with arrowheads pointing outwards at both ends
A line drawn thinner in the middle than at the edges
A line with inward arrowheads at both ends
A line with a single outward arrowhead

items.why: The concave lens is drawn as a straight vertical line whose arrowheads point inwards, towards the principal axis.

items.stem: A convex lens forms an image of a distant tree on a screen. Where does the light change direction?

options.text: Only at the surface where the light leaves the lens
At the shiny front face, where light is reflected
As it enters the lens and again as it leaves
Only at the middle, where it is thickest

items.why: A lens has two surfaces and refraction happens at both, which together bring the parallel rays from the tree to a focus.

items.stem: An object is placed between a convex lens and its principal focus, as in a magnifying glass. What sort of image is formed?

options.text: A real image, inverted and larger than the object
A virtual image, upright and larger than the object
A virtual image, upright but smaller than it
A real image formed at the principal focus

items.why: Inside the principal focus the rays leaving the lens are still diverging, so the image is virtual, upright and magnified.

items.stem: How can you tell that an image formed by a lens is real rather than virtual?

options.text: It appears the same way up as the object does
It can be seen by looking through the lens
It can be caught on a screen put where it forms
It is on the same side of the lens as the object

items.why: A real image is formed where rays of light actually meet, so a screen placed there shows it.

items.stem: In a ray diagram for a convex lens, how is the ray from the top of the object to the centre of the lens drawn?

options.text: It is bent so that it passes through the principal focus
It is curved to follow the two faces of the lens
It is bent back to run parallel to the principal axis
It carries straight on, with no change of direction

items.why: At the centre the faces of the lens are effectively parallel, so the ray emerges travelling in its original direction.

items.stem: In a ray diagram for a concave lens, a ray arrives parallel to the principal axis. How is it drawn after the lens?

options.text: Spreading away from the principal axis
Bending in to reach the principal focus beyond
Carrying straight on to the far side of it
Bending inwards to cross the principal axis

items.why: A concave lens diverges the light, and only the line traced backwards passes through the principal focus.

items.stem: An object 5 mm tall produces an image 15 mm tall. What is the magnification?

options.text: 3, from 15 mm divided by 5 mm
0.33, from 5 mm divided by 15 mm
3 mm, as the heights were in mm
10, from 15 mm minus 5 mm

items.why: magnification = (image height)/(object height) = 15/5 = 3, written as a plain number.

items.stem: An object 8.0 cm tall produces an image 2.4 cm tall. What is the magnification?

options.text: 3.3, since 8.0 is divided by 2.4
0.30, as the image is smaller
3.3, because a lens should enlarge
0.30 cm, from the heights in cm

items.why: magnification = (image height)/(object height) = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30, a value less than 1 because the image is diminished.

items.stem: An object is 4.0 cm tall and its image is 60 mm tall. What must be done before the magnification equation is used?

options.text: Convert one height so that both are in the same unit
Nothing at all, since a magnification has no unit anyway
Divide the two heights just as they are given
Divide the larger height by the smaller height

items.why: Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm; here 4.0 cm becomes 40 mm, giving a magnification of 1.5.

items.stem: A student draws ray diagrams for a convex lens and for a concave lens, using the same object in each. Which feature is the same in both diagrams?

options.text: Both images are turned upside down compared with the object
Both images can be caught on a screen behind
The ray through the centre of the lens is undeviated
The parallel ray goes to the focus beyond the lens

items.why: This construction rule is shared by both lenses, and is one of the similarities a comparison of the diagrams should bring out.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the colours of the visible light spectrum?

options.text: Each colour has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency
Each colour has one exact wavelength and one exact frequency
Each colour has its own wavelength but all share one frequency
All the colours share a wavelength band but differ in speed

items.why: This is the specification statement: every colour occupies a small range of wavelengths together with a matching small range of frequencies.

items.stem: What is the difference between specular reflection and diffuse reflection?

options.text: Specular reflection is from a rough surface, and diffuse from a smooth one
Specular reflection always obeys the law of reflection and diffuse does not
Specular reflection is from a smooth surface, diffuse from a rough one
Specular reflection sends light back and diffuse takes most of it in

items.why: The specification defines specular reflection as reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction, and diffuse reflection as reflection from a rough surface, which scatters the light.

items.stem: How does a colour filter work?

options.text: It reflects the unwanted wavelengths and lets the rest through
It absorbs certain wavelengths of light and transmits the others
It adds its own colour to the white light that passes through
It changes the wavelength of the light passing through it

items.why: This is the specification statement: filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and colours, and transmitting the other wavelengths and colours.

items.stem: What determines the colour of an opaque object viewed in white light?

options.text: The wavelengths that the object absorbs most strongly of all
The wavelengths that the object gives out when it is warm
The wavelengths that the object lets through itself
The wavelengths that the object reflects most strongly

items.why: The specification states that the colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected; the rest are absorbed.

items.stem: Which statement is true of objects that transmit light?

options.text: They must be colourless as well as see-through
They transmit light only when very smooth
They are either translucent or opaque
They are either transparent or translucent

items.why: This is the specification statement: objects that transmit light are either transparent or translucent.

items.stem: Red light and violet light both lie within the visible spectrum. Which statement about their bands is correct?

options.text: The red band lies at one fixed wavelength and the violet at another
The red band has longer wavelengths, so it has lower frequencies
The red band has longer wavelengths but the same frequency
The red and violet bands cover the same range of wavelength

items.why: Each colour holds its own band of wavelength and of frequency; red sits at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the visible spectrum.

items.stem: A mirror shows a clear image of a lamp, but a sheet of white paper beside it looks equally bright from every direction. Why does the paper behave differently?

options.text: Its rough surface obeys no law, so the rays leave at random angles
Its rough surface takes in the light and gives it out slowly
Its rough surface transmits light while the mirror reflects it
Its rough surface scatters light into many directions

items.why: Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering — diffuse reflection — so light leaves towards every viewing position and no image is formed.

items.stem: White light is shone through a blue filter. What emerges from the filter, and why?

options.text: All the colours, but with the blue much brighter than the rest
White light that has been dyed blue as it travelled through
Blue light, because the other wavelengths are absorbed by it
Blue light, because the other colours reflect back off it

items.why: White light contains every wavelength; the blue filter absorbs all of them except the blue band, which it transmits.

items.stem: A jumper appears white when it is lit by white light. What is happening to the light that falls on it?

options.text: All wavelengths are reflected equally
All wavelengths are absorbed equally by it
All wavelengths pass straight through the wool
Only the wavelengths of white are reflected

items.why: The specification states that if all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white.

items.stem: A piece of card looks black in a brightly lit room. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The light passes straight through the card without stopping
The card reflects every wavelength that falls upon it equally
The card absorbs all of the wavelengths of light that fall on it
The card gives out no light of its own in the lit room

items.why: The specification states that if all wavelengths are absorbed the object appears black, because almost no light is reflected to the eye.

items.stem: Frosted bathroom glass lets light into the room, but no clear image can be seen through it. How is the glass best described?

options.text: Translucent, since it scatters the light passing through
Transparent, since the light gets through the glass easily
Opaque, since there is no clear image to be seen through it
Specular, since the rough surface reflects light

items.why: Light is transmitted, so the glass is not opaque, but the scattering destroys the image — which is exactly what translucent means.

items.stem: A book cover appears red in white light. Which explanation of its colour is correct?

options.text: Red is absorbed by the cover and other wavelengths reflected
Red is reflected and the other wavelengths absorbed
Red is transmitted through the cover and the rest reflected
Red light is given out by the cover in any conditions

items.why: Differential treatment of the wavelengths gives the colour: the red band is reflected most strongly and the wavelengths not reflected are absorbed.

items.stem: In white light a leaf looks green and a daisy petal looks white. Which explanation accounts for both?

options.text: The leaf absorbs green strongly and reflects the other wavelengths; the petal absorbs the whole range
The leaf reflects green and absorbs the others; the petal absorbs every wavelength equally
The leaf transmits green light through itself, and the petal transmits the whole range of light
The leaf reflects green strongly and absorbs the other wavelengths; the petal reflects them all equally

items.why: Colour comes from differential reflection and absorption: unequal reflection gives green, and equal reflection of every wavelength gives white.

items.stem: A red counter is viewed through a green filter in white light. How does the counter appear?

options.text: Black, because the filter absorbs the red light it reflects
Green, because the filter turns the light green as it passes
Red, because the reflected light still gets through it
Yellow, because red and green mix inside the filter

items.why: The counter reflects only red; the green filter absorbs red, so no light reaches the eye and the counter looks black.

items.stem: White light is passed through a red filter and then through a blue filter. What is seen after the second filter?

options.text: White light, because the second filter cancels the first out
Almost no light: each filter absorbs what the other passes
Purple light, because the red and the blue light add together
Blue light, since the second filter dyes the light blue

items.why: The red filter transmits only red and absorbs the rest; the blue filter then absorbs that red, so virtually nothing emerges.

items.stem: A blue mug is placed in a darkroom lit only by red light. How does the mug appear?

options.text: Purple, since the red light mixes with the mug's own blue
Blue, since the mug keeps its colour in any lighting
Black, as there is no blue light for it to reflect
Red, since the mug absorbs the red light and shows it

items.why: A blue object reflects blue and absorbs other wavelengths; with only red light present the red is absorbed and no light is reflected.

items.stem: Which objects emit infrared radiation?

options.text: All objects do, whatever their temperature happens to be
Only objects hot enough to glow red, orange or white
Only objects that are warmer than the air near them
Only objects that have a dull, matt black surface

items.why: All bodies (objects), no matter what temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation.

items.stem: What happens to radiation that is incident on a perfect black body?

options.text: Most is absorbed, but a small part is reflected
It is all absorbed and stays trapped in the body
All of the radiation is absorbed by the body
Some is absorbed, the rest passes through

items.why: A perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it, reflecting and transmitting none.

items.stem: (HT only) Which factors does the temperature of the Earth depend on?

options.text: Only how close the Earth sits to the Sun in space
Only the distance of the Earth from the Sun and its orbit
Only how much radiation the Earth takes in from the Sun
The rates of absorption and emission, and reflection to space

items.why: The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including the rates of absorption and emission of radiation and reflection of radiation into space.

items.stem: A perfect black body would be the best possible emitter of radiation. Why?

options.text: It stores the radiation it absorbs and lets it out later
Its surface is black, and black surfaces look hottest
It reflects and transmits only a tiny amount
A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter

items.why: Since a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.

items.stem: An ice cube at −15 °C is put on a plate in a warm room. Which statement about the ice cube is correct?

options.text: It absorbs radiation but is much too cold to emit
It emits radiation, but it absorbs more than it emits
It only absorbs, because the room around it is warm
It emits no radiation until it warms up to 0 °C

items.why: All bodies emit radiation; the cube is colder than the room, so absorption outweighs emission.

items.stem: A lamp filament is heated from dull red to bright white. How does the radiation it emits change?

options.text: Only the intensity rises; the wavelength range is unchanged
Only the peak shifts; the intensity stays the same
The intensity rises and the peak moves to shorter waves
The intensity rises and the peak moves to longer waves

items.why: Both the intensity and the wavelength distribution of the emission depend on the temperature of the body.

items.stem: (HT only) A metal plate inside a hot oven has reached a constant temperature. What does this tell you about the radiation?

options.text: It absorbs radiation as fast as it emits it
It has stopped absorbing and emitting any radiation
It still absorbs radiation but no longer emits any
No radiation is absorbed or emitted now

items.why: A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation.

items.stem: (HT only) The temperature of a body is rising. Which statement must be true?

options.text: It absorbs and emits radiation at the same rate
It is absorbing radiation and emitting none at all
It is absorbing radiation faster than it emits radiation
It is absorbing radiation, and emission cannot cool it

items.why: The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.

items.stem: Two identical iron blocks are held at 30 °C and at 80 °C in the same room. Which statement about the infrared radiation they emit is correct?

options.text: Neither block emits until it is hotter than the room air
The 80 °C block emits more radiation in a given time
Both emit equally, since the blocks are identical
Only the 80 °C block emits any radiation at all

items.why: The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time.

items.stem: Two stars are the same size. Star A looks blue-white and star B looks red. What can be concluded?

options.text: Star B is hotter, since red light carries more energy
Star A is cooler, as blue light has a shorter wavelength
They are equally hot but made of different gases
Star A is hotter, and its peak wavelength is shorter

items.why: The wavelength distribution depends on temperature: the hotter star peaks at shorter wavelengths.

items.stem: (HT only) The ground cools quickly on a clear night, but much less on a cloudy night. Why?

options.text: Cloud radiates energy back down, so the net loss is smaller
Cloud acts as an insulating layer, stopping conduction of heat
Cloud completely stops the ground emitting radiation upwards
Without cloud, the warm air is not trapped near the ground

items.why: The ground still emits, but it now absorbs radiation from the cloud as well, so the imbalance is smaller.

items.stem: (HT only) An energy-balance diagram shows short-wavelength radiation arriving from the Sun and long-wavelength radiation leaving the Earth's surface. Why is the outgoing radiation longer in wavelength?

options.text: The radiation loses energy as it travels up through the air
The surface of the Earth is far cooler than the Sun
The atmosphere stretches the waves as they pass through
Only long waves can escape into space from the ground

items.why: The wavelength distribution depends on the temperature of the body, and the surface is far cooler than the Sun.
